sky.name: Sky
sky.description: The first four cells gather major celestial figures: Tinia, the supreme god comparable with Zeus and Jupiter; Cilens, often associated with Tinia; Thufltha, whose function remains debated; Nethuns, securely compared with Neptune and Poseidon; and Uni, a major goddess comparable with Juno and Hera.

water.name: Water
water.description: The next four cells include Tecum, an obscure figure connected with dedications around Lake Trasimeno; Lusal, whose reading and identity are debated; Nethuns, securely compared with Neptune and Poseidon; and Catha, an astral deity whose solar or lunar character is debated.

earth.name: Earth
earth.description: A terrestrial grouping connected with vegetation, boundaries, and earth-related divine powers. Its agricultural and boundary meanings are interpretive rather than fixed translations.

underworld.name: Underworld
underworld.description: A chthonic grouping of earth, protective, and underworld-associated names. It may relate to death, protection, and liminal passages, but individual meanings vary in certainty.

pars_familiaris.name: Pars Familiaris
pars_familiaris.description: The familiar or favorable side of the model, including names often read as domestic, attendant, or beneficent. Its omen value is part of the interpretive framework.

gall_bladder.name: Gall Bladder
gall_bladder.description: The bile reservoir is a charged divinatory area containing Tvnth, Maris, Laran, Lethams, and Nethuns. Several identifications in this zone remain debated.

central_section.name: Central Section
central_section.description: The central zone contains Hercle, Maris, Lethams, Metlvmth, and Tluscva. It combines better-documented divine names with obscure forms whose status remains uncertain.

pars_hostilis.name: Pars Hostilis
pars_hostilis.description: The hostile or unfavorable side of the model, including boundary, chthonic, and difficult-to-identify names. Its unfavorable force is an interpretive category.

back.name: Back
back.description: The back contains the Sun and Moon labels, commonly read as celestial anchors for the model's cosmological structure.

6.readingNote: The traces of lvsal are worn on the bronze and not always easy to follow. Scholarship disagrees whether the underlying form is best taken as a deity Lusa or as a genitive of the prophetic god Lur (lv(r)s(l), Colonna 1991).

13.readingNote: The letters are worn and damaged on the bronze, making the inscription hard to read; despite poor legibility, scholarship almost unanimously reads the form as Cels.

17.readingNote: Maggiani 1982 reads `pul`; Colonna 1991 argues the first letter is a `t` rather than a `p` and reads `tul(aras)`, an epithet of Selvans. The engraved letter itself is paleographically contested.

26.readingNote: The engraved form after `marisl /` reads `laθ` (l-a-theta) on the bronze, exactly as Maggiani published it in 1982. In discussion Maggiani himself withdrew that reading and replaced it with `lar` (genitive of Lar / Laran), followed by van der Meer 1987 and Colonna 1991 (n. 42). The lar reading is contextual rather than paleographic, in late northern Etruscan script theta and rho can be visually confused.

25.readingNote: The inscription in the gall-bladder zone is hard to discern because of corrosion and wear on the bronze surface, which complicates the reading; editors still cite the form read as tvnθ (e.g. Maggiani 1982).

secure.label: Secure identification
secure.tooltip: The Etruscan deity is securely identified in current scholarship.

probable.label: Probable identification
probable.tooltip: The Etruscan deity identification is plausible but not final.

debated.label: Debated identification
debated.tooltip: Scholars disagree about the identification of this name.

unresolved.label: Unresolved
unresolved.tooltip: No secure identification is currently given for this form.

clear.label: Clear reading
clear.tooltip: The Etruscan glyphs are clearly inscribed and read.

debated.label: Debated reading
debated.tooltip: How to read or segment the inscription is still disputed among interpreters.

unclear.label: Unclear reading
unclear.tooltip: The inscription is hard to read because of damage, wear, or corrosion on the bronze, not mainly because of scholarly disagreement about the letters.

secure.label: Secure
secure.tooltip: The Greek or Roman match is well established in current scholarship.

proposed.label: Proposed
proposed.tooltip: The Greek or Roman match is one proposal among several; not consensus.

superseded.label: Superseded
superseded.tooltip: Older equivalence preserved here as scholarship history; not endorsed by recent work.

tinia.description: Supreme sky god and father of the Etruscan pantheon. Maggiani 1982 and Colonna 1991 catalogue five inscribed regions tied to Tin, including the tinsθ locative (‘in [the house] of Tinia’), where Colonna reads celestial Nethuns hosted beside Tinia. Stevens 2009 reconstructs how the sixteen-part Etruscan heaven maps onto that rim and links Tin passages to Graeco-Roman threefold lightning (Festus/Seneca, manubiae); Capdeville 1992, Pernigotti 2018, and Gottarelli 2018 develop related cosmic grids.

cilens.description: Colonna 2012 reads Cilens as a catactonic (sub-earthly) divinity among the sanctuaries grouped in contemporary scholarship around community cults of the Umbrian/Etruscan border zone. Colonna 1991 anchors the nomenclature of the gods on this model; Maggiani 1982 publishes the inscribed forms as read on the bronze. On the Liver, Cilens is attested across several zones—paired with Tinia in one inscription and possibly appearing with the locative Cilensl, ‘in (the house) of Cilens’, in another. Older encyclopedic literature sometimes linked this name speculatively to Marziano Capella's Nocturnus, but discussion now follows Colonna and related work.

thufltha.description: Female deity present at cells 2, 20, 21. A Vulci dedication on a bronze statuette associates her with infernal Suri, complicating older Fortuna / Tyche equations. The tinsθ θvf locative places Thufltha ‘in the house of Tinia’.

nethuns.description: Water and sea god appearing across several Liver of Piacenza zones. Colonna 1991 distinguishes a ‘celestial’ Nethuns, hosted in Tinia's house and possibly governing rain and atmospheric moisture, from the chthonic / aqueous Nethuns of the bile zone (vesica fellea, per Pliny).

uni.description: Major state goddess of cities, birth, and sovereignty; some evidence also points to warlike and astral aspects, including comparisons with Astarte at Pyrgi.

mae.description: Obscure paired name in the Uni / Mae inscription. Maras 2017 lists Mae among the deities attested only on the Liver of Piacenza; function and identification remain unresolved, and older equations with Roman Maius are not supported in recent scholarship.

tecvm.description: Obscure deity known almost exclusively from the liver and from dedications in the area around Lake Trasimeno. Colonna 1976-77 connected the cult with Cel and the Trasimeno sanctuaries; function on the liver remains debated.

lusal.description: Genitive form lvsl / lvsal at cells 6 and 34. Two readings: a deity Lusa (Maggiani 1982) or, per Colonna 1991, lv(r)s(l), ‘of Lurs’, the prophetic god Lur. The Liber Linteus attestations are studied by van der Meer 2009; de Grummond 2014 reconstructs the cult from mirrors, dedications, and the linen book. The lvsal form is generally read more readily than lvsl beside velχ, yet the bronze is worn and interpreters still divide over Lusa versus ‘of Lurs’. The velχ collocation raises further questions; vel(...) has also been read as referring to an eponymous deity of Vulci, though that hypothesis remains debated.

catha.description: Astral deity, probably female (cells 8, 23). Maras 2017 still reads Catha as ‘a later counterpart of Cavatha, with marked solar features’, and Colonna 1991 links the Cathe Sans of the Orbetello mirror to a male solar Catha; de Grummond 2008 argued for a lunar Catha at Pyrgi and Moore 2018 revisits the question openly, so solar, lunar, underworld, and childbirth associations all remain in play, but Maras 2017 and Colonna 1991 still underline a strongly solar line against purely lunar or chthonic alternatives.

fufluns.description: God of wine, inebriation, and vegetation cycles.

selvans.description: God of forests, pastures, and liminal lands or boundaries; venerated as tutor finium. Per Colonna 1991, the inscription Maggiani read as pul may instead be tul, an abbreviation of the epithet tul(aras), supporting Selvans's role as guardian of boundaries.

tluscva.description: Obscure form on the Liver of Piacenza. Maggiani 2011 treats Tluschva as chthonic divinity / divine collective, probably female; Maras 2017 reads them as ‘a group of goddesses, perhaps corresponding to Nymphs or Charites’ attested also at Caere (Sant'Antonio); Colonna 1991 alternatively proposed Tluscu as an epithet of Maris (the only true hapax of the liver). Stopponi 2012 connects the cult with the Fanum Voltumnae at Orvieto.

cels.description: Cel / Cels, earth goddess connected with chthonic forces. Colonna 1976-77 is the canonical study, linking Cel with the Trasimeno sanctuaries; the liver itself has been read as a model of Cel's body.

culsans.description: Double-faced god of doors and thresholds. Colonna 1991 analyses the northern orthography Culsans as a compound culś sans, ‘Cul the genitor’; the abbreviation cvl may stand for either Cul (Bagnoregio altar) or Culsans.

alpans.description: Alpan / Alpans paired with Cul / Culsans. Colonna 1991 argues that alpan is originally an appellative meaning ‘the good / well-disposed’, semantically equivalent to Latin manus, used for chthonic divinities in eufemistic register. So alp here functions as an epithet of Cul, comparable to Janus being called bonus and manus.

vetis.description: Catactonic deity. Maras 2017 reads Vetis as the Etruscan substitution for Apollo on the Liver, derived from Latin Vedius (a variant of Veiovis); Colonna 2012 places Vetis with Cilens among the catactonic divinities of the hostile sector.

pul.description: Maggiani 1982 reads pul, interpreted as ‘sky’ in opposition to the adjacent metlum locative. Colonna 1991 questions the reading, arguing that the first letter could be t rather than p, and proposes tul(aras) as an epithet of Selvans (tutor finium).

lasl.description: Lasa / Lasl: female divine attendant often linked with Turan; fate and service roles are attested in mirror iconography (Krauskopf 2013). Older handbooks cited Roman Lares; current work generally treats that equivalence as misleading while still listing it as superseded scholarship history in the parallel table (Krauskopf 2013).

maris.description: Important but obscure deity attested as marisl in cell 26 and as mar in cells 30 and 39 (cells 30+39 communicate around the processus papillaris). Often represented as a child or youth in Etruscan evidence; Maras 2017 records Mariś at Clusium as ‘a divine child bearing the name of the Latin-Italic Mars’. Though the name shares roots with Latin Italic Mars, Maris is cultically and functionally unlike the Roman war-god, and the older one-to-one equation is no longer upheld (Simon 2006; Krauskopf 2013; Maras 2017).

laran.description: Etruscan god of war, securely paralleled with Mars and Ares. On the Liver of Piacenza he appears as the disputed second element after marisl: the bronze form is printed laθ, but Maggiani, van der Meer, and Colonna interpret it contextually as lar, linked with Lar / Laran.

tvnth.description: Uncertain deity of the gall bladder zone. Maras 2017 lists Tvnth among the deities attested only on the Liver; no firm identification has emerged in recent scholarship.

hercle.description: Major Etruscan god, equivalent of Herakles and Hercules, with protective and oracular associations. In Etruria treated as a god from the beginning, not as a hero.

metlvmth.description: Colonna 1991 reads metlumθ as a locative meaning ‘in the city / urbs’, qualifying the adjoining Lethams inscription as the ‘Lethams in the city’, parallel to the divine genitive sintagms of the Liber Linteus. He also reads the two contiguous sequences as one continuous inscription leθam(sl) metlumθ, not two unrelated divine names.

letham.description: Lethams (correct form per the Capua tile gen. ledamsul; Colonna 1991 corrects Maggiani’s earlier ‘Letham’). The name recurs widely on the model, often enough to rank as the most ‘ubiquitous’ deity on the liver, possibly genius-like, across both right and left lobes. Gender and sphere remain debated.

velch.description: vel(...) paired with Lvsl. Some readings take Vel(...) as an eponymous deity of Vulci rather than a fire / metalworking figure comparable to Vulcan; others stress a Vulcan-type parallel. Neither line is settled, and the Roman Vulcan parallel is marked here as proposed rather than secure.

satres.description: Obscure deity: function and identification remain debated; the form satres / satre is also attested in the Liber Linteus from Zagreb. A Roman parallel with Saturn survives in older literature and is flagged here only as superseded scholarship history rather than consensus (Maggiani 1982, Krauskopf 2013).

usil.description: The Etruscan sun-god, securely identified. On the back of the liver, usils marks the solar pole of the cosmological structure.

tiur.description: Tiur / Tivr, moon deity or moon / month term. Marks the lunar pole of the back, opposite Usil. Sannibale 2018 published a bronze crescent (CII 2610 bis) with a fresh dedication to Tiur, confirming the divine status of the term.
